meta.title: Who really said "If you have an apple and I have an apple and we exchange these apples then you and I will still each have one apple. But if you have an idea and I have an idea and we exchange these ideas, then each of us will have two ideas"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — George Bernard Shaw never said the apple/idea quote. It traces to a 1917 magazine ad and was popularized by Charles F. Brannan in the 1940s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you have an apple and I have an apple and we exchange these apples then you and I will still each have one apple. But if you have an idea and I have an idea and we exchange these ideas, then each of us will have two ideas'?
meta.ogDescription: Shaw never said it. The idea comes from a 1917 SYSTEM magazine ad; the apple version was popularized by Charles F. Brannan. Misattributed to Shaw by 1974.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — a 20th-century saying misattributed to him
answer.authorName: Charles F. Brannan (apple version); origin traces to an anonymous 1917 magazine advertisement
answer.sourceLine: This line is one of the internet’s many feel-good quotations pinned on Shaw with no basis. According to Quote Investigator, there is no evidence Shaw ever wrote or said it. The idea first appears in a 1917 magazine advertisement (using dollars, not apples), and the apple wording was popularized by U.S. Agriculture Secretary Charles F. Brannan in the 1940s; the saying was only ascribed to Shaw by 1974.

source.excerpt: If you have an apple and I have an apple and we exchange these apples then you and I will still each have one apple. But if you have an idea and I have an idea and we exchange these ideas, then each of us will have two ideas.
trail: Quote Investigator found no evidence George Bernard Shaw made this remark, and traces the idea to a 1917 SYSTEM magazine advertisement titled “The Difference Between Dollars and Ideas.”
The apple variant was spoken and popularized by U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Charles F. Brannan in the 1940s, per QI.
Check Your Fact confirms the quote appears nowhere in Shaw’s published works and rates the Shaw attribution false.
source.excerptNote: The oldest known ancestor, a 1917 SYSTEM magazine ad, used money rather than fruit: “You have a dollar. I have a dollar. We swap. Now you have my dollar … You have an idea. I have an idea. We swap. Now you have two ideas. And I have two ideas.”

author.name: Charles F. Brannan
author.heading: So who said it?
author.bio: Charles Franklin Brannan was a Colorado lawyer and U.S. Secretary of Agriculture (1948–1953) under President Truman. Quote Investigator credits him with popularizing — and possibly originating — the “apple” version of the swap-ideas saying in the 1940s. The underlying idea is older, appearing in a 1917 magazine advertisement using dollars rather than apples; the ad’s author is unknown.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Shaw
misattribution.intro: George Bernard Shaw is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for clever, feel-good lines he never wrote. This is one of them.

items.why: Quote Investigator located no compelling evidence Shaw said or wrote this, and Check Your Fact confirms it appears in none of his works. The attribution surfaced only by 1974, decades after Shaw’s death.

misattribution.truthLine: The concept comes from a 1917 SYSTEM magazine advertisement; the apple wording was popularized by Charles F. Brannan in the 1940s, per Quote Investigator — not Shaw.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The saying is a tidy parable about the non-rivalrous nature of ideas: physical goods are zero-sum, but knowledge multiplies when shared. That crisp economic insight, plus Shaw’s reputation for epigram, made the pairing irresistible — even though the wording traces to commercial and governmental speech, not a Shaw play or essay.
context.pull: Trade an apple, you still have one; trade an idea, you now have two.
